title: Heavy bleeding versus a minor cut
def: Heavy bleeding is blood that spurts, pools, soaks through cloth, or does not slow after 10 minutes of firm pressure; a minor cut slows and stops with pressure.
look: spurting, pulsing, or fast flowing blood
blood soaking through several layers or pooling on the ground
person pale, clammy, dizzy, or confused
a minor cut oozes and slows within a few minutes of pressure
use: Press hard and straight down on the wound with a thick pad or both hands and keep pressing. Call 911 for heavy bleeding. If it is a limb and pressure does not control it, put on a tourniquet. For a minor cut, wash, press, and cover.
not: Do not lift the cloth to check; add more on top. Do not use a tourniquet on a minor cut or on the neck.
call: Call 911 for any bleeding that will not stop with firm pressure.

title: How to apply a tourniquet
def: A tourniquet is a tight band, ideally a commercial windlass device, used to stop life-threatening bleeding from an arm or leg when firm pressure has not worked.
look: life-threatening bleeding from an arm or leg
a traumatic amputation
pressure and packing are not controlling it
use: Place the tourniquet 2 to 3 inches (5 to 8 cm) above the wound on bare skin, not over a joint. Pull the strap tight, turn the windlass until the bleeding stops, lock it, and write the time on it. If you cannot see the wound or are in a hurry, put it high and tight on the limb. Call 911.
not: Do not use it for a minor cut, on the neck, chest, or belly, or over a joint, a pocket, or a wallet. Do not loosen it once on; only medical staff do that.
steps: Call 911 and keep pressing on the wound until the tourniquet is ready.
Slip the band around the limb 2 to 3 inches above the wound, on skin, not over a joint.
Pull the strap as tight as you can and twist the windlass until the bleeding stops.
Lock the windlass in its clip and write the time on the tourniquet.
If bleeding continues, put a second one just above the first and tighten both.
call: Call 911; a tourniquet is emergency care, not a replacement for a hospital. Get trained in a Stop the Bleed or first-aid class before you need one.

title: Bleeding continues after a tourniquet
def: If blood keeps flowing after a tourniquet is on, it is usually not tight enough or not high enough, and the fix is to tighten it or add a second one.
look: blood still flowing or spurting below the band
a pulse can still be felt below it
the band slips or the windlass is loose
use: Tighten the windlass more until the bleeding stops. If it still flows, place a second tourniquet right above the first and tighten it. Pack the wound and press while you wait for help.
not: Do not remove or loosen the tourniquet to check the wound. Do not wait to ask permission; act and keep calling 911.
call: Call 911 and stay with the person; check for shock.

title: Packing a wound and pressure dressing
def: Packing means pushing gauze or clean cloth deep into a bleeding wound and pressing hard on it; it is used where a tourniquet will not work, such as the neck, armpit, or groin.
look: deep wound at the neck, armpit, groin, or the top of a limb
blood welling from the depth of the wound
a tourniquet cannot be placed above the wound
use: Push gauze or a clean cloth deep into the wound, right to the bleeding source. Keep packing until it is full, then press down hard with both hands for at least 3 minutes and then hold on with a wrap. Call 911.
not: Do not use a limb tourniquet on the neck. Do not remove soaked gauze; pack more on top. Do not wrap so tight around the neck that it blocks breathing.
call: Call 911; deep wounds to the neck, chest, or belly need a hospital.

title: Choking in a child or infant
def: For an infant under one year, a choking rescue uses five back blows and five chest thrusts, not abdominal thrusts; a child over one uses abdominal thrusts like an adult.
look: cannot cry, cough, or breathe, silent or high-pitched noise
blue lips or face
grabbing at the throat in a child
use: Call 911. For an infant, lay the baby face down along your forearm with the head lower than the body and give five back blows, then turn the baby over and give five chest thrusts with two fingers. Repeat until the object comes out or the baby becomes unresponsive. For a child, give abdominal thrusts from behind.
not: Do not do blind finger sweeps. Do not give abdominal thrusts to an infant. Do not hold an infant upside down by the legs.
call: Call 911; if the child becomes unresponsive, start CPR. Take a pediatric first-aid and CPR class before you need it.

title: CPR for a child or infant
def: CPR for children and infants keeps blood and oxygen moving; it is similar to adult CPR but uses less force, and breaths matter more because children often stop breathing first.
look: not breathing or only gasping
limp and unresponsive
blue or gray color
use: Call 911, then push hard and fast in the center of the chest at about 100 to 120 per minute: two fingers for an infant, one or two hands for a child, about one third the depth of the chest. Give two gentle breaths after every 30 compressions. Use an AED with child pads if available.
not: Do not stop until help or an AED takes over or the child breathes. Do not tilt an infant's head back too far.
call: Call 911 and follow the dispatcher; take a CPR class so you can do it with confidence.

title: Using an AED
def: An AED is a portable device that checks the heart's rhythm and, if needed, gives a shock; it talks you through each step.
look: person is unresponsive and not breathing normally
voice prompts after you turn it on
pads show where to be placed on bare chest
use: Call 911, turn on the AED, bare the chest, dry it if wet, and put the pads where the pictures show. Let it analyze and do exactly what it says; keep everyone clear when it shocks, then resume CPR.
not: Do not touch the person when it says to stand clear, and do not use pads over a medication patch or a pacemaker bump.
call: Call 911; anyone can use an AED safely.

title: Opioid overdose and naloxone
def: An opioid overdose slows or stops breathing, and naloxone (Narcan) is a medicine that can reverse it for a short time.
look: will not wake, slow or stopped breathing
blue or gray lips and skin
pinpoint pupils, gurgling or snoring sounds
use: Call 911 first. If naloxone is on hand, give it as the package directs, start rescue breathing or CPR if not breathing, and put the person on their side if they are breathing. If they wake and then fade, give another dose after two to three minutes.
not: Do not leave the person alone, and do not assume it has worn off; the drug can outlast the naloxone.
call: Call 911 even if naloxone works; overdose can return.

title: Broken bone, sprain, or dislocation?
def: A fracture is a broken bone, a sprain is a stretched or torn ligament, and a dislocation is a joint forced out of place; the field answer is the same: stabilize and get care.
look: fracture: point pain on the bone, deformity, cannot bear weight
sprain: pain and swelling at a joint, some use possible
dislocation: joint visibly out of place and will not move
numbness or a pale limb beyond the injury is an emergency
use: Stop using the limb, immobilize it in the position found with padding and a splint or sling, and apply a cool pack for swelling. Get X-rays if you cannot walk on it or the pain is intense.
not: Do not try to straighten a deformity or to pop a joint back in. Do not test it by walking.
call: Call 911 for an open wound over the break, a limb that is blue, pale, or numb, or a suspected thigh, hip, neck, or back fracture.

title: Cold baby: infant hypothermia
def: Babies lose heat fast, and a cold infant may have bright red, cold skin and very low energy, not just shivering.
look: bright red, cold skin
very low energy, weak cry, or refusing to feed
cool belly and chest in a cool room
use: Take the baby indoors, remove damp clothing, and hold the baby skin to skin under dry blankets, with the head and a hat covered. Warm the room. Get urgent care at once.
not: Do not use a hot bath, heating pad, or a hot water bottle, and do not put a sleeping baby in a cold car or on a cold floor.
call: Call 911 or get urgent care now for a cold, limp, or hard-to-wake baby.

title: Frostbite: what not to do
def: Frostbitten skin is numb and easily damaged; rubbing, high heat, or thawing then re-freezing makes it worse.
look: pale, waxy, hard, or blotchy skin that is numb
tingling and then loss of feeling
blisters after warming
use: Get out of the cold, take off wet gloves and boots, and gently warm the area with warm (not hot) water or body heat, such as fingers in the armpits. Do not walk on frostbitten feet if you can avoid it. Cover loosely and get care.
not: Do not rub with snow or hands, do not use a stove, fire, heating pad, or hot water, and do not thaw it if it might freeze again.
call: Get medical care for any frostbite; call 911 for confusion, shivering that stops, or deep, hard, or blackened skin.

title: Cold-water shock and near-drowning
def: Cold-water shock is the gasp and panic in the first minute after falling into very cold water, and it can cause drowning before hypothermia sets in.
look: a sudden gasp, rapid breathing, and panic
swimming ability lost within minutes
numb hands and arms that will not grip
use: Float and control your breathing for the first minute before you try to swim or climb out. Keep your head up, get out of the water as soon as you can, and then get dry, warm, and into shelter. Anyone rescued should be seen by a clinician.
not: Do not thrash or try to swim hard right away, and do not go onto the ice to help without a rope or pole.
call: Call 911 for anyone who was under water or is unresponsive; start CPR if not breathing.

title: Talking to a 911 dispatcher
also: what to say when I call 911
def: When you call 911, stay on the line and give your location and what happened; the dispatcher will tell you what to do next.
look: your exact location, with a road, landmark, or GPS coordinates
what happened and how many people are hurt
whether the person is awake and breathing
use: Call 911, say where you are, and say what happened. Answer the dispatcher's questions, and follow their instructions. Put the phone on speaker so you can help the person while you talk. Do not hang up until they tell you to.
not: Do not hang up first, and do not assume the call is placed if you have no signal; try text-to-911 or move to a place with signal.
call: If you have no cell service, try texting 911, move to higher ground, or use the satellite SOS feature of your phone.

title: Describing symptoms clearly to a clinician
also: medical history for an emergency crew
def: Clear information helps a clinician decide fast: when it started, what makes it worse or better, what medicines and allergies the person has.
look: start time and how it began
what makes it better or worse
medicines taken, allergies, and past conditions
use: Write down or say the time it started, the main symptom, any change since, medicines and allergies, and any vital signs. Keep a list of medicines and allergies in your phone or on the family card.
not: Do not guess at a diagnosis; say what you see and feel.
call: Call 911 for chest pain, trouble breathing, or any sudden severe symptom.

title: Medication basics: missed dose, expired, sharing
also: can I take this with that
def: For a missed dose, an expired medicine, or a drug interaction, read the label and ask a pharmacist; never share prescription drugs.
look: label directions for a missed dose
an expiration date
a new medicine alongside others
use: Check the label or the pharmacist or Poison Control line for a missed dose, and keep medicines in a cool, dry place. Ask a pharmacist before mixing medicines. Keep a list of what you take.
not: Do not take someone else's prescription, double up without advice, or use a medicine that looks or smells changed.
call: Call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 or 911 for an overdose or a bad reaction.

title: Lyme disease signs after a tick bite
def: Lyme disease is spread by blacklegged (deer) ticks, and an expanding red rash, often with fever, chills, and aches, can appear three to thirty days after a bite.
look: a red expanding rash, sometimes with a clear center
fever, chills, headache, and tiredness
joint pain or facial droop later
a rash is not always a bullseye
use: Remove the tick with fine-tipped tweezers, clean the bite, and note the date. See a clinician if a rash, fever, or aches follow within about a month, and say you had a tick bite.
not: Do not use nail polish, heat, or petroleum jelly on a tick, and do not wait for a bullseye.
region: Blacklegged ticks are common across Maine, Rhode Island and the rest of New England; check yourself, children, and pets after time in leaf litter, brush, and tall grass.
call: Get care for a rash or fever after a tick bite; call 911 for severe headache, stiff neck, or heart symptoms.

title: Preventing tick bites
def: Preventing tick bites means covering skin, using repellent, and checking your whole body after being outdoors.
look: tick season from spring through fall, with nymphs most active in late spring and summer
brush, leaf litter, and tall grass
small ticks the size of a poppy seed
use: Wear long pants tucked into socks, use an EPA-registered repellent or permethrin-treated clothing, walk in the center of trails, and check your body, hair, and gear. Shower within two hours and put clothes in a hot dryer.
not: Do not rely on one check; look again in the days after.
region: In Maine and Rhode Island the blacklegged tick is active whenever it is above freezing, not only in summer.
call: Call a clinician for a tick that was attached for more than a day, or any rash or fever after a bite.

title: Snakebite in New England
def: New England has very few venomous snakes: the timber rattlesnake and the northern copperhead in a few southern areas; most snakes are harmless.
look: venomous bites leave two puncture marks with swelling and severe pain
timber rattlesnake has a rattle and a heavy body
most bites in New England are from harmless snakes
use: Move away from the snake, stay calm, remove rings and tight items, and keep the bitten limb still at about heart level. Call 911 or get to a hospital; note the time and the snake's appearance if it is safe.
not: Do not cut the bite, suck it, apply ice or a tourniquet, drink alcohol, or try to catch the snake.
region: Timber rattlesnakes are rare and protected in parts of New England, and copperheads occur in southern Connecticut and Massachusetts; check state wildlife agency pages for ranges.
call: Call 911 or go to an emergency room for any bite you think is venomous.

title: Nail or tool puncture wound
def: A puncture wound is narrow and deep, closes quickly, and traps germs, so it can get infected and may need a tetanus shot.
look: a small hole with little bleeding
pain that gets worse in the next days
redness, swelling, or drainage
use: Let it bleed a little, wash with soap and clean water, and cover. See a clinician the same day for a deep wound, a rusty or dirty object, or a wound in the foot. Ask about a tetanus shot.
not: Do not seal it with glue or tape, and do not probe it. Do not ignore a puncture through a shoe.
call: Get care for deep punctures, and for fever, spreading redness, or swelling later.

title: High blood sugar (diabetic emergency)
def: High blood sugar builds slowly with thirst, frequent urination, tiredness, and fruity breath, and it can become a medical emergency.
look: extreme thirst and frequent urination
nausea, belly pain, and fast deep breathing
fruity breath and confusion
use: If the person has diabetes, help them follow their own plan and check their blood sugar. Give plain water and get medical help for vomiting, drowsiness, or fast deep breathing.
not: Do not give sugary drinks if blood sugar is already high, and do not give insulin that is not theirs.
call: Call 911 for confusion, vomiting, trouble breathing, or unresponsiveness. If you are unsure whether it is high or low and they can swallow, giving sugar is safer.

title: Ear or sinus pain after a swim or a cold
def: Ear or sinus pain after swimming or a cold is often a mild infection, but severe pain, fever, or discharge needs a clinician.
look: ear pain that hurts when you pull on it
stuffy nose and pressure around the eyes
fever, drainage, or hearing loss
use: Keep the ear dry, use a warm compress, and take over-the-counter pain medicine as the label says. See a clinician if pain lasts more than a day or two or if there is fever or drainage.
not: Do not put cotton swabs or objects into the ear, and do not use drops if the eardrum might be torn.
call: Get care for severe pain, high fever, swelling behind the ear, or dizziness.

title: Frostnip versus frostbite
def: Frostnip is a mild cold injury that turns skin pale and numb but is reversible with warming; frostbite is a deeper freeze injury.
look: frostnip: pale or red skin that tingles and returns to normal when warmed
frostbite: hard, waxy, numb skin that stays white or gray
blisters appear later with deeper injury
use: Get inside or out of the wind, cover the area with a warm dry glove or hand, and warm it gently. If skin stays numb or hard, treat it as frostbite and get care.
not: Do not rub the skin, and do not use direct heat.
call: Get care for numb, hard, or blistered skin, and call 911 if the person is confused or very cold.

title: When to start CPR
also: not breathing what do I do
def: Start CPR for anyone who is unresponsive and not breathing, or only gasping, and call 911 first.
look: no response to a shout or shoulder tap
not breathing, or only occasional gasps
no obvious signs of life
use: Call 911 or have someone call, push hard and fast in the middle of the chest at 100 to 120 per minute, about 2 inches (5 cm) deep for an adult, and let the chest rise fully. Do not stop until help or an AED takes over.
not: Do not stop to check for a pulse for long, and do not be afraid of hurting them; chest compressions can save a life. Do not do CPR on someone who is breathing normally.
call: Call 911, put the phone on speaker, and follow the dispatcher; take a CPR class for hands-on skills.
